01 · Product model

One rule connects the creator and the fan.

PlayBook aimed to keep the relationship between creators and fans continuous across content platforms. Tasks, collectible items and crafting rules offered ways for fans to express participation. The product needed to complement existing channels and lead people back to the creator’s content.

I designed Studio’s UX and UI, alongside the App’s UX flows and interaction states. Another designer created the App’s visual UI. Both sides shared a core challenge: a freely configured rule must become understandable when someone uses it.

Studio

Configure

Creators organise campaigns, tasks, items and crafting rules.

App

Participate

Fans find tasks in a creator’s community and acquire items.

Community

Express connection

Collecting, using and displaying items reflects the relationship with the creator.

02 · Studio

Show the logic while the rule is being edited.

The rule editor places required inputs, optional inputs, conditional branches and outputs on one canvas. In the source example, a gamepad and battery are required, while a supercharger is optional. Selecting it changes how an output attribute is calculated.

This structure makes the relationship between inputs and outcomes traceable. Its trade-off is canvas complexity: greater flexibility makes it more important to test whether first-time creators can find the entry point, explain their rule and correct mistakes.

PlayBook Studio · Recipe editorRebuilt in code, 2026 · interface from the source

Free to play with

Build a crafting recipe yourself

There is no fixed order. Drag any of the eight items on the left into Require, Optional or Output; anything placed can be moved again or taken out.

  • Drag: items go into the three areas; a placed item can be dragged to another area or group, or back to the library to remove it.
  • Click: And / Or toggles on a click; click a placed item to change its probability or order below the canvas, or to make its group “choose 1 out of N” (clicking the frame of the group does the same).
  • No dragging needed: click an item on the left, then the area it goes to, or use the buttons below the canvas.
Tobie’s note

What creators needed to see was the rule itself: what to hand in, what comes out, which one of several. That is why it is drawn as blocks to move around rather than as a form.

This was rebuilt in code in 2026 from the source design and the recordings of the time; it is not a deliverable from the time, and the interface elements are taken from the source: the item library, title bar and bottom toolbar are the recording itself, the eight item icons are cut from the same frame, and the three areas, item tiles, And / Or and probability bars are redrawn to the sizes and colours measured on it (UX and UI are both my work). How many items each area takes, how many fit in a group, the buttons below the canvas for probability and order, and the “reads as” line were decided for this rebuild; the source does not show them. The Condition area and the toolbar are not used in this recording and are only shown as they were. Text on the canvas uses a font from your device, not the source typeface.

PlayBook Studio · Items and their relationship webRebuilt in code, 2026 · interface from the source

Free to play with

Open an item and see what it connects to

Click items in the library. The paper crane and the red headphones have a detail view; items in the relationship web can be dragged around, and a click follows a line to the other item.

  • Click: the paper crane and the red headphones open a detail view; the source drew none for the other 32, and the demo says so.
  • Drag: items in the web can be moved, and the lines follow.
  • Follow a line: click the headphones in the crane’s web to get to the headphones, and back again. The red tab folds the detail panel away or brings it back.
Tobie’s note

Whether an item is worth keeping often depends on what it can become and what it comes from. The relationship web shows that inside the item detail, without opening the recipe list.

This was rebuilt in code in 2026 from the source design and the recordings of the time; it is not a deliverable from the time, and the interface elements are taken from the source: the page is the recording itself, the items in the web are cut from the same frames, and the lines are redrawn with the direction and colour they have there (UX and UI are both my work). The source drew a detail view only for the paper crane and the red headphones; the other items have no data and none was made up. At the bottom edge of the recording, the headphones’ web shows one more blue line and half an item that cannot be made out; they are left out. Dragging items in the web and clicking through to another item were added for this rebuild.

PlayBook Studio · Commenting on a remix submissionRebuilt in code, 2026 · interface from the source

Free to play with

Pin a comment to a place on the image

Drag a box on the image, or just click a spot, then write a line and send it. You can leave several markers, and each dot can be dragged somewhere else.

  • Drag a box or click: mark the place you mean, and the reply box opens next to it.
  • Send: the area collapses into a dot that carries your line; click the dot to fold or unfold it.
  • Adjust: a dot can be dragged to another place; the list below the image removes markers one by one, or all at once.
Tobie’s note

When a creator reviews a fan submission, a comment should land on a specific place in the image, not on “the picture” in general.

This was rebuilt in code in 2026 from the source design and the recordings of the time; it is not a deliverable from the time, and the interface elements are taken from the source: the image is the recording itself, the reply box is cut straight from it, and the selection, the dot and the bubble are rebuilt from it (UX and UI are both my work); their position and text follow what you do. The limit of 5 markers, dragging a dot, and the list below the image were decided for this rebuild; in the recording the panel on the right does not gain a new entry, so it is left alone here too. What you type stays on this page until it is reloaded; nothing is uploaded.

03 · App

Make the cost clear before the fan confirms.

An early direction explored a more game-like “furnace” interaction. Product discussions led me toward a more direct recipe-browsing flow: inspect requirements, understand readiness, then confirm consumption and possible outcomes.

Missing materials, requirements met and confirmation are distinct states. Even quick crafting needs to make the consequence clear before the user commits.

04 · Context & discovery

Keep community context coherent, but discovery open.

Home, items and missions need to answer the same question: whose community is this? I treated creator selection as shared context so related content remained coherent.

I initially favoured search within a single creator’s world. In the October 2023 product reviews, creator collaboration emerged as a central goal. We moved toward a dedicated global search covering creators, items, recipes and users, retaining local context for everyday tasks.

Tobie’s note

Consistent context helps people orient themselves. A boundary that is too strict can prevent the connections the product needs.

05 · Feedback & collaboration

Small progress should not always interrupt.

In reviews, I argued that routine tasks and significant achievements should not receive equally intrusive feedback. Frequent full-screen dialogs interrupt the experience. Lighter feedback can support everyday progress, while valuable rewards keep an intentional claim step.

Screens, states and interaction demonstrations brought these trade-offs into product discussions and supported product and investor communication. The design made abstract rules concrete enough for the team to examine together.

06 · Outcome & reflection

The team could discuss behaviour, not just screens.

The delivery included Studio UX/UI, App UX flows and states, and demonstration prototypes. Team changes interrupted further improvements before a complete development hand-off, so this case presents design and prototype outcomes.

Next, I would test a recipe from both sides: can a creator explain the rule they just made, and can a fan predict its cost and result before confirming? Understanding, completion and recovery matter more than screen count.
